title: What the First Humans Ate
description: A calm walk through the diet of our Paleolithic ancestors, based on Wikipedia sources. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleolithic, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter-gatherer, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cro-Magnon, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human

beats.narration: I wake before dawn, the air still cool, and hear the rustle of grasses around our camp. Our small band has already gathered firewood for the day ahead.
beats.caption: Dawn on the steppe
beats.image_prompt: stick figure holding a stick, small fire beside

beats.narration: Our first task is to collect edible plants—nuts, seeds, and wild berries that grew in the surrounding woodlands. We know which ones are safe from generations of observation.
beats.caption: Gathering plants
beats.image_prompt: stick figure bending, basket of berries

beats.narration: While some of us gather, others keep watch for animal tracks. The Paleolithic people lived in small societies, moving as bands that relied on both hunting and gathering.
beats.caption: Band on the move
beats.image_prompt: two stick figures, one pointing at footprints

beats.narration: We carry simple stone tools, knapped from flint, to cut and scrape. Wood, bone, and even leather are fashioned into useful implements, though they rarely survive for us to see.
beats.caption: Stone tools ready
beats.image_prompt: stick figure holding a sharp stone

beats.narration: The diet is balanced: plant foods give us roughage and vitamins, while the fat from animal meat supplies essential energy for our active lives.
beats.caption: Balanced diet
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with plant and meat icons

beats.narration: Even before the fire, we would eat raw meat or fish when we could find it, but now we roast a small piece over the flame, savoring the new taste.
beats.caption: Cooking meat
beats.image_prompt: stick figure turning meat on a fire

beats.narration: Around eighty thousand years ago, some hunter‑gatherer bands began to specialize, focusing on a narrower set of resources while expanding the tools they used.
beats.caption: Specialized bands
beats.image_prompt: two stick figures with fishing net and spear

beats.narration: They crafted fishing hooks, nets, and bone harpoons, allowing them to exploit rivers, lakes, and coastal waters for a reliable source of protein and fat.
beats.caption: Fishing innovations
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with hook pulling fish

beats.narration: In richer environments, such as the Pacific Northwest or the Osipovka culture sites, groups could stay in one place year‑round, feeding on abundant fish stocks.
beats.caption: Sedentary fishers
beats.image_prompt: stick figure beside river with fish

beats.narration: Elsewhere, on the mammoth steppes of Siberia, people hunted large game—mammoths, bison, and woolly rhinoceroses—using spears, spear‑throwers, and coordinated drives.
beats.caption: Mammoth hunt
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with spear, large outline of mammoth

beats.narration: These varied diets illustrate the flexibility of hunter‑gatherers: wherever water, plants, or game existed, humans adapted their meals accordingly.
beats.caption: Dietary flexibility
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with plant, fish, and meat icons

beats.narration: The broad spectrum approach meant no single food dominated; instead, groups consumed a mosaic of resources, balancing calories, nutrients, and seasonal availability.
beats.caption: Mosaic diet
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with puzzle pieces of food

beats.narration: Sometimes we find a carcass left by a predator. In the Lower Paleolithic, many scholars argue that early humans relied heavily on scavenging before mastering the hunt.
beats.caption: Scavenging find
beats.image_prompt: stick figure beside animal carcass

beats.narration: We strip the meat with stone blades, taking what we can before the bones are claimed by vultures or other scavengers.
beats.caption: Stripping meat
beats.image_prompt: stick figure using stone to cut meat

beats.narration: In forested areas, we also collect seafood, eggs, nuts, and fruits, showing that early diets were not limited to large game alone.
beats.caption: Forest bounty
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with egg and nut

beats.narration: When the opportunity arises—say a trapped animal—we use spears or simple traps to secure fresh meat, turning a chance kill into a shared feast.
beats.caption: Fresh kill
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with spear next to fallen animal

beats.narration: Our ability to adapt, whether hunting, fishing, or scavenging, kept our bands alive through the glacial cycles that marked the Pleistocene.
beats.caption: Adapting to climate
beats.image_prompt: stick figure under snowflake

beats.narration: Even today, the echo of that flexibility lives on in the varied dishes we prepare, a reminder of our deep‑time relationship with the land.
beats.caption: Legacy today
beats.image_prompt: stick figure cooking modern pot

beats.narration: Stone tools are the hallmark of the Paleolithic, but early humans also fashioned wooden spears, bone needles, and leather straps to aid food preparation.
beats.caption: Beyond stone
beats.image_prompt: stick figure holding wooden spear

beats.narration: Bone harpoons appear around eighty thousand years ago, indicating a growing reliance on aquatic resources, especially in coastal sites like Blombos Cave.
beats.caption: Bone harpoons
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with harpoon

beats.narration: Engraving tools and drilling implements suggest that people not only ate but also crafted ornaments, perhaps using dyed plant fibres for clothing.
beats.caption: Ornamental work
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with bead

beats.narration: Temporary huts made of branches and hides provided shelter while groups moved, and larger structures of mammoth bones show the ingenuity of Upper Paleolithic peoples.
beats.caption: Mammoth huts
beats.image_prompt: stick figure beside bone wall

beats.narration: These technologies allowed humans to process tougher foods, extract marrow, and preserve meat, extending the usefulness of each kill.
beats.caption: Processing meat
beats.image_prompt: stick figure cracking bone

beats.narration: The cumulative knowledge of tool use—what archaeologists call the ratchet effect—made each generation more efficient at turning raw resources into meals.
beats.caption: Ratchet effect
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with upward arrow

beats.narration: I sit by a fire now, thinking of the thousands of years before me when small bands roamed the world, each meal a negotiation with nature.
beats.caption: Reflecting by fire
beats.image_prompt: stick figure sitting by fire

beats.narration: Our ancestors ate what the land offered—roots, berries, fish, and the occasional mammoth—balancing calories, fat, and roughage to survive.
beats.caption: Ancient menu
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with mixed food icons

beats.narration: The shift from pure hunting to broad‑spectrum foraging, from scavenging to specialized fishing, shows a remarkable adaptability that defines us.
beats.caption: Adaptive shift
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with arrows pointing to plant and fish

beats.narration: Today, our plates are filled with foods from every continent, many of them cultivated, yet the instinct to seek variety remains.
beats.caption: Global plates
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with globe and plate

beats.narration: Understanding the first humans’ diet reminds us that nutrition is a story of environment, technology, and culture intertwined.
beats.caption: Nutrition story
beats.image_prompt: stick figure with book and food

beats.narration: As the fire dims, I wonder: what will future generations consider ‘natural’ food, and how will they look back on our choices?
beats.caption: Future reflections
beats.image_prompt: stick figure looking at distant horizon
